title: All is His power
hookLine: by His power we see and hear, by His power fear and joy (Asa di Var, ang 464)

lines: YOU DIDN'T DESIGN ANY OF IT.
ONE WORD, IN NEARLY EVERY LINE.
cards: Hold your hand up to a window and look at it. The skin, the lines across the palm, the faint pulse at the wrist. You didn't design any of it.
You didn't decide to have eyes that could see it, or a brain that could wonder about it. Yesterday Guru Nanak stood in front of creation and could only say wonder.
Today, in the salok right after, he names the force running through every piece. One word, returning in nearly every line: kudrat.

teach.b: Kudrat is a word Punjabi shares with Persian and Arabic. It means power, the power to make and to do, and in everyday Punjabi it also came to mean nature, the created world itself.
Both meanings hum in this salok, on ang 464. Guru Nanak begins with the senses. By your power we see, by your power we hear.

teach.h: IN SEEING, HEARING, FEAR AND JOY.
teach.b: By your power there is fear, and there is joy, the very core of happiness. Then the list widens. Your power is in the worlds below and the skies above, in every form.
It's in the scriptures, he says, naming the Vedas and Puranas and the Semitic books alike. It's in eating and drinking and getting dressed. It's in love.
It's in every species and color, in air and water and fire, in the dust of the earth. And then a line that can surprise.

teach.h: IN GOOD DEEDS AND IN BAD.
teach.b: Your power is in good deeds, and in bad ones. Honor and pride, too. Guru Nanak doesn't keep a clean list of pleasant things.
Everything that happens, happens inside this one power. The salok ends by turning to the One: all is your kudrat, and you are kaadir, the powerful Creator.

Kaadir and kudrat sound alike, almost a signature: the power and the Powerful belong together. The last line says Nanak sees the One at work within the hukam, the divine order, utterly alone and beyond all.
So the point isn't fear of a strong God. It's attention.

If power is in the seeing, your next glance is part of it. If it's in the eating, lunch is part of it. A Sikh walking through an ordinary day, the salok suggests, never leaves the creation's workshop.

how: Sikhs hear this salok when Asa di Var is sung in the gurdwara at dawn, and the word kudrat is common in everyday Punjabi for nature and the created world.

o: power, and the nature it makes
the luck that decides who wins
a ruler's power over his lands

games.q: inside the salok of power — tap the pairs.
p: seeing and hearing, by His power
the order the One works within

s: the salok lists only pleasant things as God's power
it names good deeds and bad ones, honor and pride, all inside the one power.
in everyday Punjabi, kudrat can also mean nature
power, and the created world that power makes.
the salok names several scriptures as part of His power
the Vedas, the Puranas and the Semitic books alike.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, standing in wonder at the world. how do you go on from wonder?
o: name the world piece by piece as the One's power.
turn away from the world to look only inward.
games.why: he lists the senses, the skies, scriptures, food, colors, good and bad, and says of each: kudrat, your power.

practice: Look at a single leaf, real or remembered, and follow one vein from stem to edge. Inside it, right now, light is becoming food and water is rising, with no one's help; then look at your own hand and notice the same quiet work.
If you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.

wordCard.voice: Kudrat. Power, and the creation that power makes. In Guru Nanak's salok, it runs through seeing, hearing, eating, loving, and every color on earth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kudrat, power; in Punjabi also the created world, nature.

carryVoice: Your line: his power. It's in the seeing, so it's in this moment too. See you tomorrow.
